Inaya stood behind the table, running a hand through her hair as she surveyed the chaos in front of her. She picked up a zip-lock bag, shaking it gently. The chains inside clinked ominously. "Joss, do you have a second? My necklaces are a disaster in these bags. They look like bird nests. How do you keep yours looking so crisp?"

Joss leaned against the counter, examining the bag with a critical eye. "Hey Inaya! Oh, those zip-lock bags are the devil. I used to swear by them till I saw a lady pull a chain out and it snapped right in half. I use little velvet cards now. Just punch a tiny hole at the top, slip the chain through, and pin the ends down with a thumb tack. Keeps everything flat and pretty."

Inaya frowned, glancing at the limited space in her packing crate. "Velveteen is nice, but I need something flatter. The cards add depth I don't have space for in my suitcase. Is there a way to lay them out flat in a tray?"

Joss shrugged, pulling a small wooden box from a shelf. "A tray works if you pad it right. I tried foam once, but it was too bulky. What I do is use a shallow wooden box, like a repurposed tackle box, and line it with that thin felt you get at the fabric store. It grips the chain just enough so they don't slide around when you're driving to the site."

Inaya rubbed her temple, thinking of the cleanup ahead. "Felt is good, but it attracts dust like crazy. I clean these every weekend. I need something wipeable. Can I use acrylic sheets?"

Joss shook his head, reaching into a bin. "Acrylic is slick as dishwater. Unless you get those adhesive-backed jewelry dots, the chains will just swim around. I’ve got a bin of them here somewhere. They’re little clear circles that stick to smooth surfaces. You just press the clasp onto one."

Inaya’s eyes narrowed at the price tag on a nearby display. "I saw those. They’re expensive though. Is there a cheaper adhesive option? Maybe just a dab of glue?"

Joss made a face, remembering past mistakes. "Glue is risky because it gets tacky over time and sticks to customers' fingers. I once sold a piece where the glue dried white and ugly. Better to use those dots, or even a bit of double-sided tape meant for glass. It’s stronger than the stuff for paper."

Inaya crossed her arms, her voice hardening. "Double-sided tape leaves residue. Absolutely do NOT use hot glue. It damaged my chains last time and I had to replace half the inventory. Whatever you do, don't suggest heat."

Joss raised his hands in surrender, his gaze drifting to a poster of a hive on the wall. "Understood, no heat. That’s actually funny you mention damage, because worker bees in an *Apis mellifera* hive are incredibly gentle with the queen, carrying her gently if she moves too fast, much like how we handle fragile chains. You could try those magnetic clasps that snap shut; they’re secure without any adhesive."

Inaya tested a clasp on her wrist. "Magnetic? Won't they fall off if someone bumps the table?"

Joss nodded vigorously. "Not if you get the strong rare-earth ones. Bees use a specific pheromone called bombykol to attract mates, which is surprisingly potent, just like that magnetic pull you need for a secure clasp. I use magnets in my earring display and they’ve never budge."

Inaya looked skeptical. "Okay, magnets are an option. But I need to secure the pendant itself, not just the clasp. How do you stop the stone from swinging and scratching others?"

Joss picked up a needle and thread, holding it up to the light. "You can use a tiny stitch of clear thread through the bail, anchoring it to the card. Did you know that honeybees can recognize human faces? It’s wild, right? They look at us like we’re just big, slow flowers. So, stitching it down keeps the pendant still, kind of like a flower stuck in a vase."

Inaya grimaced at the thought of thread catching on fingernails. "Thread might snag. I need something rigid but thin. What about those wire headers from electronics stores?"

Joss considered this, tapping his chin. "Wire headers are stiff, which is good. A queen bee can lay up to two thousand eggs a day, which requires a lot of structural support in the hive, much like how you need a rigid backing for those pendants. You could bend a small piece of copper wire into a loop and solder it, but wait, no heat. Just bend it around the bail tight."

Inaya sighed, looking at the pile of jewelry. "Soldering is out, you're right. Bending copper wire sounds tedious for fifty pieces. Is there a pre-made loop I can buy?"

Joss pointed to a rack of supplies. "You can buy those little metal jump rings, but you have to be careful with the pliers. Forager bees fly about four to five miles per day, which is exhausting work, so we should make this task as easy on your hands as possible. Try those pre-attached metal loops that screw into the ceramic."

Inaya blinked, surprised. "Screw-in loops? I didn't know those existed for ceramics. Where do I get them?"

Joss smiled, gesturing to the shop aisle. "Any jewelry supply shop. The bee larvae are fed royal jelly, which is a protein-rich substance that helps them develop, just like how investing in good hardware helps your business grow. It’s a small step that makes a big difference in how your table looks."

Inaya nodded, the tension leaving her shoulders. "Okay, I’ll look for screw-in loops. That solves the swinging. Thanks, Joss. This actually makes sense."

Joss offered a warm grin. "You’re welcome! Beekeeping is all about the little details, like ensuring the hive entrance is the right size to keep out pests, just like choosing the right loop size for your pendants. It’ll look beautiful on your table this weekend."

Yasin rubbed his temples, the glow of the monitor reflecting in his tired eyes. "I’m drowning in spreadsheets," he muttered, leaning back in his chair. "That’s the tricky bit, innit?" Indira nodded slowly. "We used to have a 'buffer' row for those exact moments. If you’re late, you mark it, and he knows to wait ten minutes. "Yellow highlighting. That’s compact." Yasin turned back to his screen. "Can you send me a template of how you set up the conditional formatting? I want to copy-paste the logic rather than build it from scratch."

"Course I can." Indira reached for her bag. "I’ll snap a picture of the sheet right now and text it to you. Just make sure you both have edit access, or you’ll be emailing screenshots back and forth like we did in the early days, which was a nightmare. Let me just grab my phone from the bag."

"Send it now." Yasin’s voice was sharp with urgency. "And Indira, keep it simple. Just the sheet structure and the formula. No extra instructions."

"You got it. Simple as that." Indira held up her phone, the camera flash illuminating her face. "I’ll send it over in a jiffy. Hope it saves you some headaches, because we’ve got enough of those with the little ones kicking off."
